etymology: An emphatic form of duh (the cartoon sound of a slow wit, 1940s), with no borrowed from the older sarcastic no kidding; American schoolyard slang by the early-to-mid 1980s for "obviously; anyone could see that." Often extended as no duh, Sherlock, mocking the speaker who announces the obvious as if he had solved a case. Still heard in American teen speech, alongside well, duh and the later Captain Obvious.
biblical_def: No duh is the Gen X reply to anyone who states the obvious: "It’s raining." "No duh." It is a small eye-roll in two syllables, a way of saying, "Why would you even tell me that?" Sometimes it is friendly teasing; often it carries a sting, because it makes the other person feel slow for speaking. The Christian observation is twofold. First, our words to one another are meant to be gracious: "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt" (Col 4:6), and "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" (Pro 15:1). A little brother who says the obvious is usually trying to join the conversation, and the eye-roll shuts the door on him. Second, there is something that really is obvious, and the world still misses it. "The heavens declare the glory of God" (Psa 19:1); God’s invisible things "are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made," so that men "are without excuse" (Rom 1:20). Yet "the fool hath said in his heart, There is no God" (Psa 14:1). The most obvious truth in the universe is the one men work hardest to deny. A father can teach his son two things with this phrase: be patient with people who say plain things, and never be the man who stands under the stars and misses what any child can see — that God made it all, and that He sent His Son to save the people who forgot Him.
webster_summary: Gen X schoolyard reply (by the mid-1980s) meaning "obviously," with an eye-roll attached; Scripture asks for gracious speech (Col 4:6) and names the one truth so obvious that men are without excuse for missing it (Rom 1:20).
webster_full: NO DUH, interj. (Gen X slang, early-to-mid 1980s, United States) Obviously; of course; you didn’t need to say that. "The test is tomorrow?" "No duh — it’s been on the board all week."
Extended forms: no duh, Sherlock; well, duh; later echoed by Captain Obvious.
Built on duh, the cartoon sound of dimness; the no is borrowed from the older sarcastic no kidding.
No entry in Webster 1828; the phrase is 20th-century American schoolyard slang.
Decode for parents: the phrase is mostly a shrug, but it can make a younger sibling feel stupid for speaking — teach grace toward the person who says the obvious.
scriptures: Col 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
Psa 19:1
The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
Rom 1:20
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
Psa 14:1
The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good.
corruption_summary: No duh makes the speaker of plain things feel slow; Scripture asks for speech seasoned with grace, and reserves its own "obviously" for the God whose power is clearly seen in all He has made.
corruption_paragraphs: The eye-roll in a word. Most uses of no duh are harmless banter, but the phrase is built to make someone feel small for speaking. A household where every plain remark is met with "no duh" teaches children to stay quiet rather than risk the sting. The Lord’s people are told to season speech with salt (Col 4:6) and to give the soft answer (Pro 15:1). Patience with the obvious is a small kindness, and it is the kindness that keeps a younger brother talking to you.

The obvious men deny. Paul’s argument in Romans 1 is a holy "no duh": the invisible things of God are "clearly seen" in creation, so that men are "without excuse" (Rom 1:20). The heavens preach every night (Psa 19:1). Unbelief is not a lack of evidence but a refusal of it: the fool says in his heart, There is no God (Psa 14:1). A child who knows what no duh means already understands the charge Scripture brings against a world that will not see its Maker.
roots_summary: Imitative duh (1940s cartoons) + no from no kidding → Gen X no duh (mid-1980s) → no duh, Sherlock; Scripture’s plain truth: God clearly seen in creation (Rom 1:20).

Older American no kidding — the sarcastic "you don’t say"
Early-to-mid 1980s schoolyards: no duh — obviously

Scripture’s obvious: the heavens declare the glory of God (Psa 19:1); men without excuse (Rom 1:20)
usage: "Mom, the pizza’s hot." "No duh, it just came out of the oven."
Let your speech be alway with grace (Col 4:6) — even toward the one who states the obvious.
The most obvious truth is the one most denied: the heavens declare the glory of God (Psa 19:1).

etymology: Imitative of a slow-witted grunt; American, heard in animated cartoons and radio comedy of the 1940s as the stammer of a dim character puzzling something out. In the late 1970s and 1980s Gen X turned it around: duh (or well, duh) became a retort meaning "that is obvious," implying the other person is the slow one. It peaked in the late 1980s and early 1990s, the era of The Simpsons (from 1989), whose Homer made the related self-directed groan D’oh! famous while Bart’s generation used duh as a reflex.
biblical_def: Duh began as the cartoon sound of a dim mind and became a weapon: say it back to someone, and you have called him stupid without using the word. "Which way is the gym?" "Duh — where it’s always been." Gen X, raised on cartoons and sitcoms, used it as a reflex, and the Simpson family made the whole tribe of grunts a national language. The Christian observation is that our Lord took name-calling of this kind more seriously than any schoolyard does. "Whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire" (Mat 5:22). Raca was an Aramaic word for an empty-head — very nearly a first-century duh. James marks the inconsistency of a tongue that blesses God and then curses "men, which are made after the similitude of God" (Jas 3:9). The gospel also turns the word upside down. "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1Co 1:27); His Word "giveth understanding unto the simple" (Psa 119:130); and to anyone who feels slow He promises, "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not" (Jas 1:5). God never says duh to an honest question. A father can tell his son: when you are tempted to make someone feel stupid, remember Who made him, and remember how patiently your heavenly Father answers you.
webster_summary: Imitative cartoon grunt of the 1940s turned Gen X retort meaning "that’s obvious"; our Lord treats the empty-head insult seriously (Mat 5:22), and God gives wisdom to all who ask, upbraiding not (Jas 1:5).
webster_full: DUH, interj. (Gen X slang, late 1970s–1990s, United States; older cartoon origin) An exclamation that the thing just said is obvious, implying the speaker is slow. "Is it Friday?" "Duh."
Forms: well, duh; no duh; duh-uh, drawn out for emphasis. Cousin of Homer Simpson’s D’oh! (1989 onward), which is aimed at oneself.
Earlier sense (1940s cartoons and radio comedy): the stammer of a dim-witted character.
No entry in Webster 1828; the word is a 20th-century American imitative interjection.
Decode for parents: duh is a way of calling someone stupid without the word; the Lord who forbade Raca (Mat 5:22) cares about it.
scriptures: Mat 5:22

But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
Jas 3:9
Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Jas 1:5
If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.
corruption_summary: Duh calls a brother an empty-head in one syllable; Christ warned against that very insult (Mat 5:22), and the Father answers every honest question without upbraiding (Jas 1:5).
corruption_paragraphs: Contempt in one syllable. The power of duh is that it insults without seeming to: no bad word was said, yet the hearer knows he has been called stupid. Our Lord saw through that trick long ago. Raca — empty-head — brought a man before the council (Mat 5:22), because contempt for a brother is murder’s small beginning. A tongue that sings on Sunday and sneers on Monday is the double tongue James rebukes, blessing God and cursing the men made in His likeness (Jas 3:9).

The God who never says duh. Every child asks questions that seem obvious to adults, and every believer asks God questions that must seem the same. Yet the Father gives wisdom "liberally, and upbraideth not" (Jas 1:5); His Word gives understanding to the simple (Psa 119:130); and He chooses the foolish things of the world to confound the wise (1Co 1:27). A home that reflects Him will be a place where no honest question earns a duh.
roots_summary: Imitative grunt of a slow wit (1940s cartoons) → Gen X retort duh / well, duh (1980s) → Simpsons era (1989 onward); Scripture: say not Raca (Mat 5:22); God upbraideth not (Jas 1:5).

usage: "Did you know the mall closes at nine?" "Duh."
Whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council (Mat 5:22).
If any of you lack wisdom, ask of God, who upbraideth not (Jas 1:5).

etymology: Yeah (informal yes; compare the KJV yea, from Old English gea) + right, said flatly or with a drawn-out vowel so that two agreements mean a refusal: "I don’t believe you." Sarcastic yeah, right is older American speech, but it became a Gen X signature in the 1980s and 1990s beside as if and Not!; the classroom joke that it is "the double positive that makes a negative" circulated widely in the same years.
biblical_def: Yeah, right is a yes that means no. "I’ll clean the garage this weekend." "Yeah, right." The tone does all the work: the words agree, the voice scoffs. It was Gen X’s default reply to promises from parents, politicians, and advertisers, and there is a hard-won honesty in it — that generation had heard a great many promises broken. The Christian observation is that Scripture records this exact tone at some of the turning points of redemption. When the Lord promised a son to a woman of ninety, "Sarah laughed within herself" (Gen 18:12) — a yeah, right if ever there was one — and the Lord answered, "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" (Gen 18:14). When Elisha promised bread in a starving city, the king’s officer sneered, "if the LORD would make windows in heaven, might this thing be?" and was told, "thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof" (2Ki 7:2). Skepticism toward men is often wise; skepticism toward God is unbelief, and "without faith it is impossible to please him" (Heb 11:6). The remedy is not to pretend we never doubt, but to bring the doubt to Him, like the father who cried, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief" (Mar 9:24). A father can tell his child: say yeah, right to the salesman if you must; never say it to God, because every promise He has made in Christ is yea and amen.
webster_summary: Gen X sarcastic reply ("I don’t believe you") in which two agreements make a refusal; Scripture hears the same tone in Sarah’s laugh and answers, Is any thing too hard for the LORD? (Gen 18:14).
webster_full: YEAH, RIGHT, interj. (Gen X slang, 1980s–1990s, United States) Said flatly or with a drawn-out vowel: I don’t believe that for a moment. "He says he’ll be on time." "Yeah, right."
Companions: as if, Not!, sure you will; the classroom joke calls it the double positive that makes a negative.
Distinct from the sincere yeah, right ("yes, correct"), which differs only in tone.
Webster 1828: YEA, adv. Ya. 1. Yes; a word that expresses affirmation or assent. …
Decode for parents: the phrase is useful skepticism toward men and deadly unbelief toward God; teach your child which is which.
scriptures: Therefore Sarah laughed within herself, saying, After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?
Is any thing too hard for the LORD? At the time appointed I will return unto thee, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son.

Then a lord on whose hand the king leaned answered the man of God, and said, Behold, if the LORD would make windows in heaven, might this thing be? And he said, Behold, thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof.
Heb 11:6
But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
Mar 9:24
And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
corruption_summary: Yeah, right turns yes into a sneer; Scripture records that sneer in Sarah’s laugh and the officer of Samaria, and answers that nothing is too hard for the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Earned skepticism, misplaced. Gen X learned its yeah, right honestly: broken homes, broken promises, and a television that sold everything. Suspicion of men’s promises is often prudence. But a habit of sarcasm does not stop at the salesman. Aimed upward, it becomes the laugh of Sarah (Gen 18:12) and the scoff of the officer who saw the miracle with his eyes and never tasted the bread (2Ki 7:2). Unbelief always believes it is simply being realistic.

The cure for unbelief. Scripture does not shame the honest doubter; it shows him where to take his doubt. The father in Mark 9 did not hide his yeah, right; he confessed it with tears: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief" (Mar 9:24). Christ healed his son. Faith is not pretending the promise is easy to believe; it is trusting the God who made it, and that trust is what pleases Him (Heb 11:6).
roots_summary: Old English gea (KJV yea) → informal yeah → sarcastic yeah, right (Gen X peak, 1980s–90s); Scripture: Is any thing too hard for the LORD? (Gen 18:14).

Is any thing too hard for the LORD? (Gen 18:14) — the answer to every heavenward yeah, right.
Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief (Mar 9:24).

etymology: American slang of the early 1990s, picturing a conversation as a road and the unwelcome subject as a place one refuses to travel. Popular in African American and youth speech of the period and spread nationally by 1990s sitcoms and daytime talk shows, usually with a raised palm (the companion gesture of talk to the hand). Variants: don’t even go there, let’s not go there, I’m not going there.
biblical_def: Don’t go there draws a line across a conversation: that subject is off limits. Said with a raised palm, it can be a joke between friends, a warning before a fight, or a wall around a wound. The Christian observation is that Scripture itself says don’t go there — and means it — about some roads. "Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil men. Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away" (Pro 4:14-15). Some old offences should stay buried, too: "He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends" (Pro 17:9), and "where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth" (Pro 26:20). A wise child learns not to go to gossip, to the old quarrel, or to the website his father has warned him about. But there is one place the phrase must never be used, and that is with God. The heart is full of rooms we would rather keep locked, and we say don’t go there to the Holy Spirit as often as we say it to our friends. The psalmist did the opposite: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts" (Psa 139:23). Christ already knows what is in the locked room, and He went to the cross for it. A father can teach both halves: refuse to go where sin lives, and never refuse God entrance to any part of you.
webster_summary: Early-1990s American phrase (often with a raised palm) declaring a subject off limits; Scripture says it of the path of the wicked (Pro 4:14) and forbids saying it to God, who searches the heart (Psa 139:23).
webster_full: DON’T GO THERE, interj. (Gen X slang, early 1990s, United States) Do not raise that subject; leave that alone. "You want to talk about my report card? Don’t go there."
Variants: don’t even go there, let’s not go there, I’m not going there; often with a raised palm, kin to talk to the hand.
The figure: a conversation as a road, and certain subjects as places one does not travel.
No entry in Webster 1828; the phrase is late-20th-century American slang.
Decode for parents: when your teenager says it, there may be a wound behind the wall — respect the moment, and keep the door open for later.
scriptures: Pro 4:14
Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil men.
Pro 4:15
Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away.
Pro 17:9
He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:
corruption_summary: Don’t go there can wisely close the road to gossip and old quarrels, or foolishly lock a room of the heart against the God who searches it.
corruption_paragraphs: A good fence. Not every use is a sin. Proverbs is full of places a wise man does not go: the path of the wicked (Pro 4:14-15), the repeated grievance that separates very friends (Pro 17:9), the talebearer’s fire that dies when no one feeds it (Pro 26:20). A teenager who says don’t go there to a dirty joke or a piece of gossip is doing exactly what Solomon told his son to do. Some roads are best never started.

A locked room. The danger is the same phrase turned inward. Men build walls around their pet sins and old hurts and post a sign: don’t go there. Friends learn to stay out; so, they hope, will God. But no room is hidden from Him, and the believer’s prayer is an open door: "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psa 139:23). What a man will not let Christ enter, he will not let Christ heal.
roots_summary: The conversation as a road → early-1990s American don’t go there (with raised palm) → don’t even go there; Scripture: go not in the way of evil men (Pro 4:14), but Search me, O God (Psa 139:23).

Biblical roads: avoid the path of the wicked (Pro 4:15); open the heart to God (Psa 139:23)
usage: "Remember that haircut you had in seventh grade?" "Don’t go there."
Enter not into the path of the wicked (Pro 4:14) — the right place to say it.
Search me, O God, and know my heart (Psa 139:23) — the place never to say it.

etymology: African American conversational and comic speech, carried nationally in the early-to-mid 1990s by sitcoms, stand-up comedy, and daytime talk shows, usually delivered with a pointed finger and rising pitch. It expresses outrage, real or mock, at an insult, a bold move, or a scandalous bit of news. Later variants oh no she didn’t and oh no he didn’t became stock lines of reality television.
biblical_def: Oh no you didn’t is outrage as theatre. Someone insults your mother, cuts in line, or wears the same dress to prom, and the room erupts: "Oh no you didn’t!" Most of the time it is comedy — half the fun is the performance — but it also announces that an offence has been taken and a reply is coming. The Christian observation is that God gives a different script for the moment after an insult. "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression" (Pro 19:11). "A wrathful man stirreth up strife: but he that is slow to anger appeaseth strife" (Pro 15:18). James sets the order: "swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (Jas 1:19). That does not mean nothing is ever wrong; "Be ye angry, and sin not" (Eph 4:26) allows real anger at real evil. But the phrase is often shouted by bystanders enjoying a quarrel that is not theirs, and Proverbs has a word for that: such a man "is like one that taketh a dog by the ears" (Pro 26:17). The greatest offence in history was the cross — sinful men crucified the Lord of glory — and He answered, "Father, forgive them" (Luk 23:34). A father can let his son laugh at the comedy, teach him to refuse the crowd that cheers a fight, and show him the glory of passing over a wrong.
webster_summary: 1990s exclamation of mock outrage from African American comic speech, now everywhere; Scripture’s script for the moment after an insult is slower: it is a man’s glory to pass over a transgression (Pro 19:11).
webster_full: OH NO YOU DIDN’T, interj. (Gen X slang, early-to-mid 1990s, United States) An exclamation of outrage, real or mock, at an insult or bold act. "She said your cooking tastes like cardboard?" "Oh no she didn’t!"
Forms: oh no she didn’t, oh no he didn’t; delivered with a pointed finger and rising pitch.
Origin in African American conversational and comic speech; carried nationally by 1990s sitcoms, stand-up, and talk shows.
No entry in Webster 1828; the phrase is late-20th-century American slang.
Decode for parents: half comedy, half fight-starter; teach your children not to be the crowd that cheers a quarrel.
scriptures: The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression.
A wrathful man stirreth up strife: but he that is slow to anger appeaseth strife.
Jas 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
Eph 4:26
Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:
He that passeth by, and meddleth with strife belonging not to him, is like one that taketh a dog by the ears.
corruption_summary: Oh no you didn’t turns an offence into a show and a quarrel into entertainment; Scripture calls it a man’s glory to pass over a transgression.
corruption_paragraphs: Offence as entertainment. The phrase is funny because it is a performance, and the audience is part of the act. That is also its danger. A culture trained by talk shows to enjoy a confrontation will cheer the fight it ought to stop, and Proverbs likens the meddler in another man’s strife to someone grabbing a dog by the ears (Pro 26:17). Christians are called to be the peacemakers in the room, not the chorus that makes the quarrel louder.

The glory of the unsaid reply. God’s wisdom runs against the crowd here: "it is his glory to pass over a transgression" (Pro 19:11). The slow-to-anger man is not weak; he is the one who calms the strife (Pro 15:18). Anger has a lawful place (Eph 4:26), but the Lord Jesus, reviled on the cross, did not revile in return. The Christian’s highest reply to an insult is not a finger in the air but forgiveness.
roots_summary: African American comic and conversational speech → 1990s sitcoms, stand-up, talk shows → reality-TV stock line; Scripture: it is his glory to pass over a transgression (Pro 19:11).

Biblical counter-script: slow to wrath (Jas 1:19); pass over a transgression (Pro 19:11)

The discretion of a man deferreth his anger (Pro 19:11).
Swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath (Jas 1:19) — the reply that ends the show.

etymology: From snap, a sharp, cutting joke in the African American verbal contest variously called the dozens or snaps; to snap on someone is to roast him, and the 1994 book Snaps collected the form for a national audience. Oh, snap! — the bystander’s cry when someone lands a sharp comeback, or when something suddenly goes wrong — was common in hip-hop and urban youth speech by the early-to-mid 1990s and was revived by Millennials in the 2000s. The older English snap means a quick bite or a sudden crack.
biblical_def: Oh, snap! is the crowd’s cry when a comeback lands: one boy roasts another, the cut is sharp, and everyone in earshot shouts it. It can also mean simple surprise — "Oh snap, I forgot my homework" — but its home is the verbal contest, where the quickest tongue wins. The wit of the dozens is real, and the culture that sharpened it deserves credit for its speed and invention. The Christian observation is that Scripture knows exactly how sharp a tongue can be and tells us what to do with the edge. "There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health" (Pro 12:18). "Death and life are in the power of the tongue" (Pro 18:21). The apostle forbids "corrupt communication" and commands speech "good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers" (Eph 4:29). Proverbs speaks to the bystander, too: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth" (Pro 24:17). The oh snap crowd rejoices in exactly that stumble. Paul warns where the game ends: "if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another" (Gal 5:15). A father need not take the fun out of quick wit; he should aim it. Teach your son to be quick to build up, quicker to stand beside the boy being roasted, and slow to cheer when someone falls.
webster_summary: 1990s hip-hop and urban exclamation (from snap, a cutting joke in the dozens) cheering a sharp comeback or a sudden surprise; Scripture: Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth (Pro 24:17).
webster_full: OH SNAP, interj. (Gen X slang, early-to-mid 1990s, United States) An exclamation at a sharp insult or comeback; also at any sudden surprise or mishap. "He said your jump shot looks like a sneeze? Oh, snap!"
From snap, n., a cutting joke in the verbal contest called the dozens or snaps; to snap on someone is to roast him.
Millennial revival in the 2000s; softened to a mild "oops" in everyday use.

Webster 1828: SNAP, v.t. 1. To break at once; to break short; as substances that are brittle. Breaks the doors open, snaps the locks. 2. To strike with a sharp sound. 3. To bite or seize suddenly with the teeth. 4. To break upon suddenly with sharp angry words. …
Decode for parents: when your child shouts it, someone else has usually just been cut — ask who, and whether he is all right.
scriptures: There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health.
Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof.
Eph 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth:
Gal 5:15
But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.
corruption_summary: Oh snap is applause for a wound; Scripture prizes the tongue that heals and forbids gladness when another stumbles.
corruption_paragraphs: Applause for the cut. The bystander who shouts oh snap has not said anything cruel himself, but he has paid the cruelty its wages. Roasting games survive because the crowd rewards them, and the boy on the receiving end learns to laugh along while he bleeds. Solomon names the pleasure for what it is: gladness at another’s stumble (Pro 24:17). The tongue that speaks like the piercings of a sword (Pro 12:18) rarely works alone; it works for an audience.

Sharpness redeemed. Quick wit is a gift; the problem is the target. The same quickness that lands a roast can land a word "good to the use of edifying" (Eph 4:29), a defense of the weaker boy, or a ready answer to a scoffer. Paul’s warning to the Galatians is the honest end of the roasting game: those who bite and devour one another are consumed (Gal 5:15). Christ makes a man sharp for the sake of others.
roots_summary: Middle Dutch / Low German snappen (to bite quickly) → snap as a cutting joke in the dozens → 1990s hip-hop oh snap! → Millennial revival; Scripture: the tongue of the wise is health (Pro 12:18).
roots_lines: Middle Dutch / Low German snappen — to bite at, to seize quickly
English snap — a quick bite; a sharp crack; a curt retort
African American verbal contest: the dozens / snaps; the 1994 book Snaps
Early-to-mid 1990s hip-hop and urban speech: oh snap!; 2000s Millennial revival
Biblical tongue: piercings of a sword vs. health (Pro 12:18); bite and devour (Gal 5:15)
usage: "He said your mixtape sounds like a dial-up modem." "Oh, snap!"
Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth (Pro 24:17).
Death and life are in the power of the tongue (Pro 18:21) — even the bystander’s.

etymology: American teen slang by the mid-1980s, common through the 1990s in schoolyards and on television: a rude dismissal meaning "get lost; I don’t care what you think." It is generally taken as a clipped form of coarser imperatives; its exact origin is uncertain. The verb bite is Old English bitan.
biblical_def: Bite me is the Gen X way to slam a door with two words. A parent asks a question, a teacher gives a correction, a sibling makes a remark, and the answer is: "Bite me." It means, roughly, "I reject you and everything you just said," with a coarse edge most teenagers understand even if they could not explain it. The Christian observation is that Scripture uses the same picture, and uses it as a warning. "If ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another" (Gal 5:15). Biting is what animals do; Paul says that a church, or a family, that speaks this way will eat itself alive. God’s instruction for the moment of irritation is the reverse: "Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing" (1Pe 3:9). "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger" (Pro 15:1). "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men" (Rom 12:18). And the apostle puts this kind of speech on the list of things a Christian strips off like old clothes: "anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth" (Col 3:8). Christ, who had every right to dismiss us, says instead, "Come unto me" (Mat 11:28). A father should be plain: this one goes. Not because it is the worst thing a child could say, but because it is contempt in a short sentence, and contempt has no place in a home that has been shown grace.
webster_summary: Gen X rude dismissal (by the mid-1980s) meaning "get lost; I reject you"; Scripture uses the biting image as a warning — if ye bite and devour one another, take heed (Gal 5:15).
webster_full: BITE ME, interj. (Gen X slang, mid-1980s–1990s, United States) A rude dismissal: get lost; I don’t care what you think. "Clean your room." "Bite me."
Generally taken as a clipped form of coarser imperatives; origin uncertain. Kin to eat my shorts and talk to the hand.
Common in 1990s sitcom and cartoon dialogue as the stock teenage retort.

Webster 1828: BITE, v.t. preterit tense bit; participle passive bit, bitten. 1. To break or crush with the teeth, as in eating; to pierce with the teeth, as a serpent; to seize with the teeth, as a dog. 2. To pinch or pain, as with cold; as a biting north wind; the frost bites. …
Decode for parents: this one is contempt with a coarse edge; it belongs on the list of things a Christian puts off (Col 3:8).
scriptures: Gal 5:15
But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.
Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing.
Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Col 3:8
But now ye also put off all these; anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth.
corruption_summary: Bite me is contempt in two words, most often aimed at parents; Scripture warns that those who bite and devour one another are consumed, and commands blessing for railing.
corruption_paragraphs: Contempt at the door. The phrase is short because contempt does not need many words. It dismisses not an argument but a person, and in Gen X homes it was most often fired at mothers and fathers. That gives it a special weight, because the fifth commandment does not lapse at thirteen. A child who learns to answer correction with bite me is learning to answer God’s correction the same way. Put it off with the rest of the old man’s wardrobe (Col 3:8).

Families that bite. Paul’s image is exact: biting and devouring until there is nothing left (Gal 5:15). Homes are rarely destroyed in one blow; they are eaten away by a thousand small dismissals. The cure is the gospel’s contrary pattern — blessing for railing (1Pe 3:9), the soft answer (Pro 15:1), and peace as far as it lies in us (Rom 12:18) — learned from the Savior who answered our rebellion with His own life.
roots_summary: Old English bitan (to bite) → mid-1980s teen dismissal bite me (origin uncertain) → 1990s sitcom staple; Scripture: if ye bite and devour one another, take heed (Gal 5:15).
roots_lines: Old English bitan — to pierce with the teeth
Mid-1980s American teen speech: bite me — get lost; exact origin uncertain
1990s television and schoolyard staple; kin to eat my shorts
Gen X note: most often aimed upward, at parents and teachers
Biblical biting: bite and devour one another (Gal 5:15); render blessing for railing (1Pe 3:9)
usage: "You’re grounded." "Bite me." "Now you’re grounded for two weeks."
If ye bite and devour one another, take heed (Gal 5:15).
Not railing for railing, but contrariwise blessing (1Pe 3:9).

etymology: From American slang have a cow, "to become wildly upset," current by the 1950s–60s (compare the older have kittens and have a fit). The negative Don’t have a cow, man! became Bart Simpson’s catchphrase on The Simpsons (Fox, from December 1989) and was printed on a flood of T-shirts in 1990, making it one of the defining phrases of late Gen X and early Millennial childhood.
biblical_def: Don’t have a cow means "calm down; you’re overreacting," and in 1990 it was one of the most quoted sentences in America. Bart Simpson said it to his mother, his principal, and his father, usually right after doing something that deserved a strong reaction. That is the joke, and it is worth seeing clearly: the phrase is often a child telling an adult that the adult’s alarm is the problem, not the child’s mischief. The Christian observation has two sides. First, Scripture really does tell us not to have a cow. "Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil" (Psa 37:8). "Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools" (Ecc 7:9). "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding" (Pro 14:29). For the anxious heart the cure is not a shrug but prayer: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God" (Php 4:6). Parents especially need this word; a father who explodes over every spilled glass teaches nothing but fear. Second, a child does not get to set the temperature of the home. "Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right" (Eph 6:1). A father can laugh at Bart and still teach his son the difference: calm is a virtue for everyone, but it is not a weapon for waving off a mother’s correction. The Prince of Peace gives calm to both.
webster_summary: Bart Simpson’s catchphrase (1990), from 1950s–60s have a cow (to get wildly upset); Scripture agrees, Cease from anger (Psa 37:8), and reminds the child who says it to obey his parents (Eph 6:1).
webster_full: DON’T HAVE A COW, interj. (Gen X slang, 1990, United States) Calm down; don’t overreact. "Don’t have a cow, Mom, it’s only a little paint."
Bart Simpson’s catchphrase ("Don’t have a cow, man!"), The Simpsons, Fox, from 1989; a best-selling T-shirt slogan of 1990.
From have a cow, to become wildly upset (US, 1950s–60s); compare have kittens, have a fit, flip out.
Webster 1828: COW, n. plural cows; old plural kine. The female of the bovine genus of animals; a quadruped with cloven hoofs, whose milk furnishes an abundance of food and profit to the farmer. …
Decode for parents: good advice for fathers, poor manners from sons — calm is a virtue, not a way to dismiss correction.
scriptures: Psa 37:8
Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil.
Ecc 7:9
Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools.
He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly.
Php 4:6
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
Eph 6:1
Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right.
corruption_summary: Don’t have a cow carries true wisdom about anger wrapped in a cartoon’s sass toward parents; Scripture keeps the first and corrects the second.
corruption_paragraphs: Sound advice in a smart mouth. The irony of Bart’s catchphrase is that it is mostly good counsel. Anger rests in the bosom of fools (Ecc 7:9); the slow-to-wrath man has great understanding (Pro 14:29). Plenty of Gen X fathers needed to hear it. But in the cartoon the line is spoken by a boy to the adults he has just wronged, and the laugh trains children to treat a parent’s alarm as the real problem. Wisdom spoken with contempt stops being wisdom.

Peace that is not a shrug. The world’s version of calm is indifference: nothing matters enough to get upset about. The Christian’s calm is something else — anxiety taken to God "by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving" (Php 4:6), anger surrendered (Psa 37:8), and a child’s obedience offered "in the Lord" (Eph 6:1). That kind of peace keeps a household steady because it rests on Someone steadier than the household. It is not having no cow; it is having a Father.
roots_summary: Old English cu → cow; US slang have a cow (1950s–60s, get wildly upset) → Bart Simpson’s Don’t have a cow, man! (1990); Scripture: Cease from anger (Psa 37:8).
roots_lines: Old English cu → cow
US slang have a cow (1950s–60s) — to become wildly upset; compare have kittens
The Simpsons (Fox, from December 1989): Bart’s Don’t have a cow, man!
1990: the T-shirt craze makes it a national catchphrase
Biblical calm: cease from anger (Psa 37:8); be careful for nothing (Php 4:6)
usage: "Don’t have a cow, man — I’ll fix the window."
Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry (Ecc 7:9) — Bart was right about that much.
Children, obey your parents in the Lord (Eph 6:1) — the half of the lesson the cartoon left out.

etymology: Chill pill, an imaginary tranquilizer, from chill ("calm down"; see that entry) + pill; American teen slang of the early 1980s, widespread by the middle of the decade as take a chill pill — "calm down, you’re overreacting." It belongs to the same family as chill out, mellow out, and Bart Simpson’s don’t have a cow, and its picture echoes an age in which pills for mood were becoming ordinary.
biblical_def: Take a chill pill is what one teenager says to another who is getting worked up: calm down, relax, you’re overreacting. The picture is a little tablet that makes the agitation go away. The phrase is mostly harmless, and sometimes exactly right. But its picture says something about the age that coined it: a generation that grew up as pills for every mood became common learned to imagine calm as something you swallow. The Christian observation is that God offers a peace no prescription can produce. "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee" (Isa 26:3). Christ says, "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth" (Joh 14:27). The peace of God "passeth all understanding" and keeps "your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus" (Php 4:7). It does not come from a pill but from a Person, and it is reached by being still before Him: "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psa 46:10). Proverbs even names a medicine that works: "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine" (Pro 17:22). None of this forbids a doctor’s care; it simply puts the deepest calm where it belongs. A father can tell his worried daughter: there is no chill pill for the soul, but there is a Savior who stilled the sea with a word, and He is not too busy to still you.
webster_summary: Early-1980s American teen slang for "calm down," picturing calm as an imaginary tranquilizer; Scripture offers a peace not as the world giveth (Joh 14:27), found in being still before God (Psa 46:10).
webster_full: TAKE A CHILL PILL, interj. (Gen X slang, early-to-mid 1980s, United States) Calm down; relax; stop overreacting. "It’s just a quiz — take a chill pill."
Chill pill, n., an imaginary tranquilizer; from chill (calm down) + pill. Companions: chill out, mellow out, don’t have a cow.
Still in use, often shortened to chill; mildly dismissive when aimed at real distress.

Webster 1828: CHILL, n. 1. A shivering with cold; rigors, as in an ague; the cold fit that precedes a fever; sensation of cold in an animal body; chilliness. [See Cold and Heat.] 2. A moderate degree of cold; chilliness in any body; that which gives the sensation of cold.
Decode for parents: fine for a friend who is over-excited, unkind toward one who is truly afraid — and a quiet lesson that calm cannot be swallowed.
scriptures: Isa 26:3
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
Php 4:7
And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
corruption_summary: Take a chill pill pictures peace as something you swallow; Scripture gives a peace the world cannot give, kept by the mind stayed on God.
corruption_paragraphs: Calm in a capsule. The joke of the phrase is harmless, but the picture is telling. A generation that saw pills prescribed for restlessness, sadness, and sleep learned to imagine calm as a chemical. Medicine has its honest place, and Luke was a physician; but no tablet can quiet a guilty conscience or a heart that fears death. The peace Christ gives is "not as the world giveth" (Joh 14:27), because the world has nothing in its cabinet that reaches that deep.

Dismissing the afraid. The phrase also has an edge. Said to a friend who is truly frightened, it means "your fear is your problem." The Lord never speaks that way to His people. To the anxious He says, Be still, and know that I am God (Psa 46:10), and He keeps in perfect peace the mind stayed on Him (Isa 26:3). Christians can tell one another to calm down only if they also show one another where calm is found.
roots_summary: Old English ciele (cold) → chill → late-1970s chill out → early-1980s chill pill (imaginary tranquilizer); Scripture: perfect peace, the mind stayed on thee (Isa 26:3).
roots_lines: Old English ciele — cold, coolness; English chill
Late 1970s American slang: chill out — calm down
Latin pilula, little ball → English pill
Early-to-mid 1980s teen speech: take a chill pill
Biblical peace: not as the world giveth (Joh 14:27); passing all understanding (Php 4:7)
usage: "Dude, take a chill pill — the bus isn’t even here yet."
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee (Isa 26:3).
Be still, and know that I am God (Psa 46:10) — the calm no pill provides.

etymology: Old English ciele, cold. Chill out, "calm down, relax," is recorded in American speech by the late 1970s and was carried by African American youth speech and early hip-hop into the 1980s (chillin’, "relaxing, hanging out"); by the mid-1980s chill alone served as verb ("just chill"), as adjective ("he’s chill," easygoing; "that’s chill," fine), and as a word of approval. The Black American speech communities that coined it deserve the credit; it is now universal American English.
biblical_def: Chill does three jobs in Gen X speech: as a command it means "relax" ("just chill"); as a description it means easygoing ("her dad is chill"); as praise it means fine or good ("that’s chill"). The word borrowed coolness from cold weather and turned it into a whole temperament. There is much here to redeem. Scripture prizes a quiet, unhurried spirit: "In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength" (Isa 30:15). David describes a soul that has learned to be still before God: "Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother" (Psa 131:2). The Shepherd "maketh me to lie down in green pastures" (Psa 23:2), and Christ calls the weary, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mat 11:28). The Christian observation is that rest has a source; it is not a personality type but a gift received from the Lord. But the word also has a cold edge. Chill can slide from calm into indifference — nothing matters, nobody cares, whatever — and the Lord’s sharpest rebuke is for exactly that temperature: "thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot" (Rev 3:15). A father can bless his son’s easygoing manner while teaching him the difference: be at rest in Christ, but never be chill about Christ.
webster_summary: Gen X slang from African American and hip-hop speech (chill out, late 1970s; chillin’, 1980s) for relax, easygoing, or fine; Scripture gives true rest in Christ (Mat 11:28) and warns against the chill of indifference (Rev 3:15).
webster_full: CHILL, v. and adj. (Gen X slang, late 1970s–1980s, United States) To relax, calm down, hang out; as an adjective, easygoing or fine. "We’re just chillin’ at Mike’s." "Her parents are pretty chill."
Forms: chill out, chillin’, chill pill, chillax (2000s blend with relax).
Origin in African American youth and early hip-hop speech; now universal American English.

Webster 1828: CHILL, n. 1. A shivering with cold; rigors, as in an ague; the cold fit that precedes a fever; sensation of cold in an animal body; chilliness. [See Cold and Heat.] 2. A moderate degree of cold; chilliness in any body; that which gives the sensation of cold.
Decode for parents: calm is good; indifference is not — listen for which one your child means.
scriptures: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
For thus saith the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel; In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not.
Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child.
Psa 23:2
He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.
Rev 3:15
I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot.
corruption_summary: Chill names a real good, rest and quietness, but slides easily into indifference; Christ gives the first and spues out the second.
corruption_paragraphs: Rest without a source. The world’s chill is a temperament or a technique: some people are just laid-back, and the rest try to get there with music, screens, or substances. Scripture’s rest is a gift with a Giver. Christ does not merely say "relax"; He says "Come unto me" (Mat 11:28). The quietness and confidence Isaiah promised (Isa 30:15) came only to those who returned to the Lord, and Israel, the prophet adds, "would not."

The cold side of chill. A word that started with cold weather can end with a cold heart. When chill means "nothing gets to me," it has drifted from peace into apathy, and apathy toward God is the lukewarmness the risen Christ cannot stomach (Rev 3:15). A weaned child is calm because his mother is near (Psa 131:2), not because he has stopped caring. The Christian is meant to be both: at rest in the Lord and fervent for Him, quiet in spirit and hot in love.
roots_summary: Old English ciele (cold) → English chill → late-1970s chill out → 1980s hip-hop chillin’ → universal chill; Scripture: rest in Christ (Mat 11:28), not lukewarmness (Rev 3:15).
roots_lines: Old English ciele — cold, coolness
English chill — a coldness; to make cold
Late 1970s American chill out — calm down; cool one’s temper
1980s African American and hip-hop speech: chillin’, just chill; adj. chill, easygoing
Biblical rest: quietness and confidence (Isa 30:15); the danger: neither cold nor hot (Rev 3:15)
usage: "What are you doing tonight?" "Nothing, just chillin’."
Come unto me … and I will give you rest (Mat 11:28) — the only chill that lasts.
Be at rest in Christ, never chill about Christ (Rev 3:15).

etymology: From psych, a clipping of psychology / psychological (Greek psyche, breath, life, soul). Psyched up, "mentally keyed up before a contest," is American sports talk of the 1960s; by the late 1970s and 1980s Gen X used plain psyched for "thrilled, eagerly excited" about anything ("I’m so psyched for the concert"). Not to be confused with the playground taunt Psyche! ("fooled you"), which has its own entry.
biblical_def: To be psyched is to be fired up, thrilled, can’t-wait excited: psyched for summer, psyched for the game, psyched about a new car. Coaches used to psych their teams up before a big match; Gen X made the word everyday. Underneath it lies the Greek psyche, the soul, and that root is worth reclaiming, because Scripture has a great deal to say about the soul getting stirred. David commands his own soul to rise: "Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name" (Psa 103:1). He talks to his discouraged soul and lifts it with hope: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? … hope thou in God" (Psa 42:5). He was psyched for worship: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD" (Psa 122:1). Paul wants believers "fervent in spirit; serving the Lord" (Rom 12:11) — enthusiasm with a direction. And the highest excitement of all is promised, not manufactured: "in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore" (Psa 16:11). The Christian observation is that excitement is not the problem; misplaced excitement is. A child who can be psyched about a video game but bored by God has a soul pointed in the wrong direction. A father can say: be psyched about good things, and save your best gladness for the Lord’s Day and the Lord Himself.
webster_summary: Gen X adjective (from 1960s sports psyched up) for thrilled or eagerly excited; its root is Greek psyche, the soul — and Scripture shows the soul stirred to bless the LORD (Psa 103:1).
webster_full: PSYCHED, adj. (Gen X slang, late 1970s–1980s, United States) Thrilled, excited, eager. "I’m so psyched for the beach trip."
From psyched up (1960s American sports talk), mentally keyed up for a contest; psych is a clipping of psychology.
Distinct from the taunt Psyche! ("fooled you"); opposite psyched out, rattled or intimidated.
No entry in Webster 1828; psych and psyched are 20th-century American clippings of psychology.
Decode for parents: excitement is a gift; notice what your child is psyched about, and let him see what you are.
scriptures: Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name.
Psa 42:5
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance.
I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.
Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
corruption_summary: Psyched spends the soul’s enthusiasm on games and gadgets; Scripture shows the soul at its most stirred in blessing the LORD and gladly going to His house.
corruption_paragraphs: Enthusiasm without aim. A generation can be psyched about almost everything except what matters most. The same boy who cannot sleep the night before a concert yawns through worship, and he is not unusual; enthusiasm follows treasure. That is why David preaches to his own soul (Psa 103:1) rather than waiting to feel stirred. The soul can be taught where to aim its excitement, and a father’s own visible gladness in the house of the LORD (Psa 122:1) is the first lesson.

Fervent, not frantic. Paul’s phrase "fervent in spirit" (Rom 12:11) is the redeemed form of psyched: real heat, but harnessed to "serving the Lord." The world’s excitement spikes and crashes; the believer’s joy has a fixed object and a sure future — fulness of joy in God’s presence (Psa 16:11). When the soul is cast down, the remedy is not more hype but hope in God (Psa 42:5). A soul that has learned to be glad in God will still be psyched about summer, but it will not need summer to be glad.
roots_summary: Greek psyche (soul) → psychology → clipped psych → 1960s sports psyched up → Gen X psyched, thrilled; Scripture: Bless the LORD, O my soul (Psa 103:1).
roots_lines: Greek psyche — breath, life, soul
Psychology → clipped psych (early 20th c.)
1960s American sports talk: psyched up — keyed up for a contest; psyched out — rattled
Late 1970s–1980s Gen X: psyched — thrilled, eager
Biblical soul stirred: Bless the LORD, O my soul (Psa 103:1); fervent in spirit (Rom 12:11)
usage: "Are you psyched for the game Friday?" "Totally psyched."
I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD (Psa 122:1).
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? hope thou in God (Psa 42:5).

etymology: From African American women’s speech, where you go ("keep going, you’re doing great") and girl as a term of friendship were long established; you go, girl! was carried nationally in the early-to-mid 1990s by sitcoms, talk shows, and stand-up comedy, and by the end of the decade was a general American cheer of encouragement for a woman or girl. Also you go, said to anyone.
biblical_def: You go, girl! is a cheer: a friend nails a job interview, finishes a race, stands up to a bully, and her friends shout it. It is encouragement in three words, and encouragement is a thoroughly biblical thing. "Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another" (1Th 5:11). "Let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works" (Heb 10:24). Scripture itself says you go, girl to women of courage and faith. Boaz told Ruth, "all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman" (Rut 3:11). The husband of the virtuous woman praises her: "Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all" (Pro 31:29), and the chapter ends with a public cheer: "let her own works praise her in the gates" (Pro 31:31). The Christian observation is that a cheer is only as good as what it cheers. In the 1990s the phrase was sometimes shouted at a woman throwing off husband, children, or modesty, as if any act of self-assertion were brave. Scripture’s encouragement is aimed: it praises the woman who fears the LORD, works with willing hands, opens her mouth with wisdom, and does good to her household. A father should be the loudest cheerer his daughter ever has — for her courage, her kindness, her faith, her hard work — and let her know that the praise that matters most belongs to the woman that feareth the LORD.
webster_summary: 1990s cheer of encouragement from African American women’s speech, now general American; Scripture cheers women too — let her own works praise her in the gates (Pro 31:31) — but aims its praise at virtue.
webster_full: YOU GO, GIRL, interj. (Gen X slang, early-to-mid 1990s, United States) Well done; keep it up; I’m proud of you — said to a woman or girl. "You got the scholarship? You go, girl!"
From African American women’s speech: you go (keep going) + girl (friend); also you go alone, to anyone.
Carried nationally by 1990s sitcoms, talk shows, and stand-up; by 2000 a general American cheer.

Webster 1828: GIRL, n. gerl. [Low Latin gerula, a young woman employed in tending children and carrying them about, from gero, to carry; a word probably received from the Romans while in England.] 1. A female child, or young woman. In familiar language, any young unmarried woman. 2. Among sportsmen, a roebuck of two years old.
Decode for parents: encouragement is biblical (1Th 5:11); notice what is being cheered, and cheer your daughter loudly for what is good.
scriptures: Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do.
And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works:
Rut 3:11
And now, my daughter, fear not; I will do to thee all that thou requirest: for all the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman.
Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all.
Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates.
corruption_summary: You go, girl is real encouragement that can cheer anything at all; Scripture praises women warmly and aims the praise at virtue, faith, and good works.
corruption_paragraphs: A cheer without a target. Encouragement is a good gift, and the women who coined this phrase knew how to give it. The danger lay in what the 1990s often cheered: a woman leaving her vows, mocking modesty, or treating her home as a cage. When any self-assertion earns you go, girl, the cheer stops meaning "well done" and starts meaning "do what you want." Scripture provokes "unto love and to good works" (Heb 10:24), not to anything at all.

The Bible’s own cheer. Proverbs 31 ends in applause: her children rise up, her husband praises her, and her works praise her in the gates (Pro 31:28-31). Boaz honored Ruth for her loyalty and faith (Rut 3:11). These are you go, girl moments, given for courage, diligence, kindness, and the fear of the LORD. A father who learns to praise those things out loud will raise a daughter who knows what is worth cheering.
roots_summary: African American women’s speech (you go + girl) → 1990s sitcoms and talk shows → general American cheer; Scripture: let her own works praise her in the gates (Pro 31:31).
roots_lines: Middle English gurle — a child, a young person; later a young woman
African American women’s speech: girl as a term of friendship; you go — keep going
Early-to-mid 1990s: you go, girl! carried nationally by television and stand-up
By 2000: a general American cheer; you go said to anyone
Biblical praise of women: a virtuous woman (Rut 3:11); thou excellest them all (Pro 31:29)
usage: "I finally finished my nursing degree!" "You go, girl!"
